full_text:
Israeli government nods to international stabilisation force in Gaza
The ISF, to be staffed by ‘friendly countries’, will operate in areas of the Palestinian enclave that are outside Israel’s military control.
Israel’s government has approved the entry of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), part of United States President Donald Trump’s 20-point “peace plan,” to Gaza.
An Israeli official reported on Sunday that Israel’s security cabinet had approved the key legal measures and that the force would operate “in full coordination with” the Israeli military, according to the Times of Israel.

There was no timeframe given for when the ISF, which will include 200 people from “friendly countries such as Uganda and Morocco”, according to the Reuters news agency, will be deployed.
The cabinet determined that Israel will have the authority to approve which countries can send forces.
Following the implementation of Trump’s deal, Israel dictates who can and cannot enter the Gaza Strip, along with how much aid and food can enter, in the wake of Israel’s two-year, genocidal war on Gaza.
Though a “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel was agreed in October, reports of killings of Palestinians by the Israeli military occur almost daily.
The Palestinian Ministry of Health reports that 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the deal was implemented, with 3,888 wounded.
The plan also called for an international “Board of Peace” to oversee the administration and reconstruction of the strip, for the creation of a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) technocratic governing body, and for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw from the strip.
Nickolay Mladenov, the director-general of the Gaza Board of Peace – which the vast majority of Western countries refused to join – welcomed the news.
The former Bulgarian foreign minister and defence minister said Israel enabling the deployment was “a critical part of the agreed framework for stabilising Gaza, supporting demilitarisation, and enabling the transition to effective Palestinian transitional administration” under the NCAG.
The cabinet’s approval comes a day before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to travel to Washington, DC in the United States.
Israel currently occupies close to 70 percent of Gaza. Its population of almost two million has been forced to live in a diminishing fraction of the strip, as Israel continues to move the “Yellow Line” it created to demarcate areas it withdrew to under the first phase of the deal.
The ISF will operate in the areas that are not under Israeli control.

title: US and Iran hit pause on strikes for second day
summary: The relative calm comes amid reports of renewed efforts to restore diplomatic talks.
full_text:
US and Iran hit pause on strikes for second day
The relative calm comes amid reports of renewed efforts to restore diplomatic talks.
The United States and Iran have pressed pause on what had been an escalating conflict for a second day.
Reports on Sunday said neither the US nor Iran had launched strikes for a second day in a row. The sudden period of calm after two weeks of nightly attacks on Iran by the US and Iranian retaliation on US allies in the Gulf came amid hopes of a return to diplomacy.

- list 3 of 3‘Freeze the conflict’: Drones slow Kazakh oil flow amid Russia-Ukraine war
US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told Fox News on Sunday that President Donald Trump was “giving [the potential for] talks … a little bit of room”.
While noting that the president has said the US was “locked and loaded,” Waltz said negotiators have been engaged at every level over the past few weeks, and in particular, over the past few days.
US broadcaster CBS, quoting two regional sources, reported that the US decision to pause the bombing was made due to the arrival in Tehran of a delegation from Oman.
The New York Times reported that Trump paused plans to escalate attacks due to concerns about draining the Pentagon’s diminishing stockpile of missile interceptors and other air defence munitions in the Middle East.
Iran’s army, meanwhile, said it had halted its strikes in the Gulf.
“Our strategy has essentially been retaliatory. We have also halted our retaliatory operations,” Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, according to the AFP news agency.
However, like the US, Iran was also sure to maintain its bullish rhetoric, with Akraminia warning that the conflict would widen further if the US continues its attacks.
According to Turkiye’s Anadolu news agency, Pakistani and Qatari mediators have intensified communications with the US and Iran after both sides responded to a de-escalation formula to end the conflict.
Tensions in strait continue
Regarding the Omani delegation, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the talks about managing marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz – the focus of the recent outbreak of hostilities – were “useful and progress was made”.
“Technical and political consultations” are ongoing, he added.
Meanwhile, incidents in the waterway, a key export route for oil and natural gas exports from the region, continued, maintaining the risk of escalation.
The US military’s Central Command said on Sunday that its naval blockade of Iran “remains in full effect”.
It noted that as of Saturday, it had redirected 12 commercial vessels, disabled two that had not complied with directions and boarded two “to ensure total compliance”.
Iranian media reported that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps stopped six vessels from trying to transit the strait over the previous 24 hours by firing warning shots.
They also reported that an oil tanker exploded after hitting a mine in the strait. The Tasmin News Agency reported that the ship struck a mine after leaving the Iranian-approved route.
Control over the Strait of Hormuz is a point of contention between the US and Iran. Iran says it controls passage through the waterway under a memorandum of understanding that was signed by Washington and Tehran in June and established a 60-day period for the final terms of a deal to be negotiated.
The US says Iran does not control the strait and has tried to create a secondary route for vessels to transit the waterway.

Trump called Hernandez’s drug-trafficking trial a set-up by the Biden administration.
Former President Juan Orlando Hernandez has returned to Honduras from the United States after President Donald Trump pardoned him after he received a 45-year jail sentence for drug trafficking.
Hernandez returned to the Central American country on Sunday, four years after being extradited to the US. He is now due to go on trial in Honduras on fraud and money-laundering charges, but activists worry that he will not face real justice.

Arrest warrant suspended
Despite his pardon on the US charges, Hernandez is expected to appear in court on August 3 to face the Honduran charges.
However, he was not detained upon arrival in Honduras because an arrest warrant was suspended in June, and local activists are concerned that the trial will turn out to be a sham.
“Everything points to the suspension being the first step,” said Joaquin Mejia, a lawyer and researcher for the Reflection, Research and Communication Team, a human rights organisation.
“He’ll come, they’ll likely issue him alternative measures to imprisonment to keep up appearances, and then he’ll end up without any problem, without any sanction.”
“There is a social majority that is outraged but doesn’t speak out because of fear,” Mejia added “We’re talking about the boss of all drug bosses.”
Hernandez, once considered an ally by the US in its “war on drugs”, led Honduras from 2014 to 2022. During that time, he said during a meeting with drug dealers that they would “shove the drugs right up the noses of the gringos”, according to a US prosecutor at his trial in New York.
A Pandora Papers corruption investigation accused Hernandez and other high-profile officials of diverting nearly $11m in state funds to political campaigns from 2010 to 2013. Some of this money was allegedly used for Hernandez’s first presidential campaign.
Former President Porfirio Lobo and ex-Finance Minister Wilfredo Cerrato were both implicated in the same investigation, and the charges against them were dismissed.

summary:
Follow the day’s news live

Nine years ago, as deputy prime minister and Nationals MP for New England, Barnaby Joyce was instrumental in supporting a resident-backed campaign for Armidale to be a site for resettling refugees, spruiking its benefits for reducing regional skills shortages.

Last December, the area’s federal MP, Barnaby Joyce, defected from the Nationals to One Nation, saying he was “philosophically aligned” with the rightwing party.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Jacinta Allan loses majority caucus support after meeting of state Labor factions
Benita Kolovos
Speculation has been mounting overnight that Victoria’s Labor premier Jacinta Allan will face a leadership challenge this week, just four months from an election.
Factional conveners from Labor’s left and right met on Sunday night to discuss whether Allan still had the support of a majority of the caucus. It is understood the group agreed she did not.
But the pathway to a leadership challenge remains unclear as Allan’s most likely opponent – the deputy premier, Ben Carroll – has indicated to colleagues he would only run if the position was vacant.
Barnaby Joyce suggests One Nation could accept some refugees while barring other migrants
It’s also well worth watching this video of Guardian Australia’s community affairs reporter Adeshola Ore’s interview with Barnaby Joyce about Armidale’s refugee resettlement program and One Nation’s policy positions on immigration.
One Nation’s policy is that immigrants who do not speak English should “under no circumstances … be able to settle in Australia”.
However, Joyce told the Guardian there could be an exemption for refugees under a One Nation government because they are a different cohort than “general immigration”.
Nine years ago, as deputy prime minister and Nationals MP for New England, Barnaby Joyce was instrumental in supporting a resident-backed campaign for Armidale to be a site for resettling refugees, spruiking its benefits for reducing regional skills shortages.
Last December, the area’s federal MP, Barnaby Joyce, defected from the Nationals to One Nation, saying he was “philosophically aligned” with the rightwing party.
On a national level, One Nation is pushing a vision of a “monocultural” Australia alongside an anti-immigration agenda. But in the electorate of the party’s most high-profile recruit, a different story is playing out.
Key figure in Icac NSW Liberal inquiry will not appear
A key figure at the centre of an anti-corruption inquiry involving the New South Wales Liberal party has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence during eight weeks of public hearings.
The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) will start its Operation Rosny hearings on Monday. The first witness will be hotelier Michael O’Hara, followed later in the week by former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw and consultant Robert Assaf.
O’Hara and Assaf are among 10 individuals Icac has said it is investigating. Whitelaw is not named in the Icac allegations.
Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist and Liberal powerbroker who once received a glowing endorsement from the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, is named in two Icac allegations but is not expected to appear.
A 2023 parliamentary inquiry preceded Icac’s current examination of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”. Since that parliamentary inquiry, Ellis has moved to the UK, Guardian Australia can reveal.
Jacinta Allan loses majority caucus support after meeting of state Labor factions
Benita Kolovos
Speculation has been mounting overnight that Victoria’s Labor premier Jacinta Allan will face a leadership challenge this week, just four months from an election.
Factional conveners from Labor’s left and right met on Sunday night to discuss whether Allan still had the support of a majority of the caucus. It is understood the group agreed she did not.
But the pathway to a leadership challenge remains unclear as Allan’s most likely opponent – the deputy premier, Ben Carroll – has indicated to colleagues he would only run if the position was vacant.
Two more bird flu cases confirmed in South Australia
Two local birds in South Australia suspected to have a deadly bird flu, greater crested terns found in Robe and Semaphore, have been confirmed positive for the H5N1 virus by CSIRO.
This takes the total of H5 confirmed or presumed positive detections to 20 nationally, Australia’s acting chief veterinary officer, Dr Sam Hamilton, said in a Sunday statement.
All of these have been individual wild seabirds found in coastal locations.
There remains no evidence of any mass mortality events and there are no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system.
NSW planning minister calls for bill to allow commercial activity around new pool
The planning and public services minister, Paul Scully, said the Callan park upgrades represented a “new era”.
“The new tidal baths and return of 1.6 hectares, or the equivalent of 4,000 large picnic blankets of green open space, to the community will mean more people can enjoy this great parkland,” he said on Monday.
Scully argued Callan park would be further improved by the Parklands bill, which passed the state’s lower house in May and was now before the Legislative Council. Legislation currently prevents any commercial activity in Callan park.
“For the park to be able to host your new favourite café and reach its full potential, we need the … bill to pass parliament,” Scully said.
When opened, the Callan park baths will be the latest of Sydney’s new or re-animated public swimming spots. Marrinawi Cove at Barangaroo was dubbed Sydney’s first city beach in 50 years when it opened in 2023.
Bayview park on the Parramatta River reopened for swimming in 2022 after being closed for more than five decades. The river also boasts Chiswick baths and Cabarita beach, while “Pondi” – Penrith beach – was opened in Castlereagh in 2024.
Sydney’s latest harbour swimming pool, on the banks of Callan Park in Lilyfield, will open for swimmers this summer, the state government says, with construction now under way.
The new tidal baths on the Iron Cove foreshore, along the popular Bay Run and close to sports fields like Leichhardt Oval and King George Park, is expected to attract thousands to the southern banks of the Parramatta River.
Demolition work has also started on nine unsafe buildings in Callan park “which were neglected for so long that they have become not only an eyesore but a safety hazard”, the Minns government said on Monday.
“The removal of these long cordoned off buildings will unlock central parts of Callan Park, delivering the equivalent of two football fields of green space back to free community use,” the government said in a statement.
The baths will include a shark net, a fixed jetty, a pontoon, and an accessible pathway and ramp into the water.
Construction of the new tidal baths was expected to take six months, meaning it should open for summer 2026. The building demolition in Callan park was also expected to be completed by the end of this year.
Stephanie Convery will be with you soon to take you through today’s news as it unfolds.
At 2pm AEST today, most phones in the country will blare an emergency siren as part of the first nationwide test of the new AusAlert warning system. People who may have secret “safe phones”, kept hidden for personal safety reasons, have been advised to consider turning off their devices for up to 24 hours after the test and drivers have been warned not to touch their phones during the alert.
The Royal Commission on Anti-semitism and Social Cohesion continues in Sydney.
And Ed Husic is up on ABC Radio soon to talk about fallout from the national Labor conference.

title: Burnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ support
summary:
Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said underlined Britain’s “unwavering” backing for Ukraine.

Less than two weeks after Keir Starmer travelled to Kyiv for the final foreign visit of his prime ministership, the Ukrainian president will on Monday join Burnham at a naval base where Ukrainian forces have been receiving training.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said underlined Britain’s “unwavering” backing for Ukraine.
Less than two weeks after Keir Starmer travelled to Kyiv for the final foreign visit of his prime ministership, the Ukrainian president will on Monday join Burnham at a naval base where Ukrainian forces have been receiving training.
Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week, and the prime minister has promised to maintain Starmer’s strong support for the country in pushing back against Russia’s invasion.
On the visit to the base, the pair will speak to Ukrainian and British military personnel who have taken part in Exercise Sea Breeze, a 15-country training deployment based on mine exercises and other maritime operations in the Black Sea.
The second part of this year’s exercise, which took place in Portland, Dorset, finished on Friday and involved more than 200 Ukrainian personnel.
Burnham and Zelenskyy are also due to discuss joint projects including Stone Cloak, an electronic jammer for which the UK has shared the intellectual property, allowing Ukraine to use the system immediately.
Thousands of the jammers, each about the size of a tablet computer, have been sent to Ukraine to be fitted to drones, with the aim of stopping Russian air defence systems from tracking and targeting them.
Ukraine is now able to mass produce the devices itself. After being initially used there, the jammers are due to be fitted to new UK weaponry, including cruise missiles.
Burnham, in a comment released by Downing Street before the visit, said: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve a long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine.
“Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.”
According to statistics released by No 10, since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, total UK support for the country has totalled £25bn, including £16bn in military assistance.
Starmer visited Ukraine a number of times, and hosted Zelenskyy regularly. In one of the most telling displays of UK support, after a March 2025 visit to the White House during which the Ukrainian leader was publicly berated by Donald Trump, he then travelled to the UK and met not only Starmer but also King Charles at Sandringham, which is primarily a royal home and rarely used for official events.
During Starmer’s final visit to Ukraine, Zelenskyy presented him with the country’s Order of Freedom, the most prestigious honour that can be given to an overseas national.
During a press conference with Starmer, the Ukrainian president said he hoped to build a strong relationship with Burnham, and to arrange a meeting “as soon as possible”.

title: Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘fomenting hate’ in calls for PM’s arrest
summary:
Israeli prime minister says ICC’s war crime charges are ‘bogus’ and plans to be in New York for UN gathering this fall

Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, is “fomenting hate” by calling the Israeli prime minister a war criminal who should be arrested over Israel’s war in Gaza if he visits the city for the United Nations general assembly.

Netanyahu said he intends to be in New York in September to address the annual UN gathering of world leaders, despite the mayor’s suggestion that he is not welcome. Mamdani said on Wednesday that while New York City does not have legal authority to execute an arrest warrant issued by the world’s top war crimes court, he encouraged the federal government to do so.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, is “fomenting hate” by calling the Israeli prime minister a war criminal who should be arrested over Israel’s war in Gaza if he visits the city for the United Nations general assembly.
Netanyahu said he intends to be in New York in September to address the annual UN gathering of world leaders, despite the mayor’s suggestion that he is not welcome. Mamdani said on Wednesday that while New York City does not have legal authority to execute an arrest warrant issued by the world’s top war crimes court, he encouraged the federal government to do so.
“He’s supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers – Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone,” Netanyahu said on the Fox News channel’s Sunday Morning Futures with Maria Bartiromo. “But he’s trying to turn one group against the other.”
The prime minister has become an increasingly polarizing figure over Israel’s war in Gaza, which was ignited by the 7 October 2023 deadly attack on southern Israel by Hamas militants. Israel also joined the US in starting the war against Iran on 28 February before launching a ground invasion in southern Lebanon in response to fire from the Iranian-backed Hezbollah group.
Netanyahu on Sunday dismissed the international criminal court (ICC)’s war crimes charges against him as “bogus”. He pointed to sexual misconduct allegations against the ICC’s top prosecutor, who was removed from that post on Friday, and said the warrant was an attempt to divert attention.
Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.
Netanyahu on Sunday also said he was concerned that once-bipartisan political support for Israel in the US is at risk, particularly as progressive and far-left Democrats aligned with the Mamdani wing of the party splinter.
He also warned against rising antisemitism in the US and other western countries, saying that when he talks to people in New York City, home to the second-largest Jewish population in the world, “Jews feel very uncomfortable”.
“And I think it’s wrong,” he said. “The whole thing is wrong.”
Throughout his 2025 mayoral election campaign, Mamdani said he would seek to order the city’s police to execute the ICC’s arrest warrant over Netanyahu’s role in the war in Gaza.
“I want to be equally clear, Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,” he said in his video message on Wednesday.
He told New Yorkers that he understood their frustration and that expressions of protest is something the city would “always respect”.
The Hague-based court has accused Netanyahu, his former defense minister and the late leader of Hamas of crimes against humanity. The Palestinian territory’s health ministry says more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s offensive – roughly half of them women and children. About 1,200 people, most of them civilians, were killed in the initial Hamas attack on Israel.
Trump on Monday told Netanyahu in a social media post that he “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America”.
Netanyahu is expected in Washington DC on Monday to meet with Trump and attend funeral services for Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator.
Graham, a leading defense hawk and strong supporter of Israel, died suddenly on 11 July of a likely torn aorta. Netanyahu called him a “great patriot” and one of Israel’s “greatest friends”.

title: Wildfire Disruptions to the Tour de France Show How Climate Change Is Shaping Sports
summary: Tadej Pogačar's fifth Tour de France victory came after last-minute course changes due to wildfires, underscoring how climate change is influencing major sporting events.
full_text:
What should have been a standout moment in the world of sports was almost overshadowed on Sunday as 27-year-old Slovenian cyclist Tadej Pogačar took home his fifth Tour de France amid a last-minute course change in response to wildfires raging in the country’s southwest region. The disruption is one of a growing number of examples of extreme weather forcing changes to global sporting events.
For the final stage of the world’s most prestigious cycling race, what was meant to be a 133-kilometer (82-mile) ride was shortened to 89 km (55.3 miles). Riders were presented in Thoiry before being transported by team buses to Paris, where the race consisted entirely of circuits around the French capital, including two additional laps of the Champs-Élysées.
The change was announced late Saturday. Officials said it would allow emergency first responders and security personnel to shift their attention from the race to the wildfires.
"In a spirit of national solidarity with the areas and communities affected, it was decided to adapt the route for the final stage," the event's organizers said in a statement.
The disruption was just the latest in a series of extreme weather events that have altered this year’s competition. Earlier in the race, stage nine was shortened by 30 km (18 miles) due to extreme heat.
A number of the participants commented on the impact of extreme heat this year, including Pogačar, who suggested having cyclists race earlier, when the heat is less intense, or altering the race calendar.
“If I had the power I would change all the calendar and not race in July and August in hot places,” he said.
The race director replied that such a schedule shift would never be possible, as it could impact critical factors of the event, from obtaining government authorizations to negatively impacting viewership—and therefore the revenue—when the race is aired by broadcasters.
As of Saturday night, dozens of wildfires were burning in the southwest of France, near Bordeaux. Over 197,000 people had already been evacuated throughout the country, while its neighbor, Spain, saw some 80,000 evacuated.
Research shows climate change is fostering the conditions that allow wildfires to spread rapidly, as hotter temperatures and drier vegetation make many landscapes more flammable. In the last four years, the amount of land burned by wildfires across Europe increased by 57%, according to new data from the World Health Organization.
In Spain and Portugal alone, the number of wildfires has more than doubled since last year.
Europe, which is warming faster than any other continent, is in the midst of a particularly dry, hot summer, creating ideal conditions for wildfires. Following a heatwave in June, data showed that France recorded at least 5,700 excess deaths during the month.
Two weeks later, at the start of this year’s Tour de France, the average temperature along the course was 87.4°F—far surpassing the previous record of 78.6°F in 2022.
Climate Change Is Forcing Sports to Adapt
The Tour de France is not the only sporting event that’s been forced to contend with the impact of climate extremes.
“Recent years have been a turning point for sport, just because so many sporting events have been impacted by climate change,” says Madeleine Orr, assistant professor of Sport Ecology at the University of Toronto. In 2020, tennis player Dalila Jakupovic collapsed on court during the Australian Open due to poor air quality because of wildfires. Soon after, the Tokyo Olympics saw athletes sweltering in 90°F temperatures.
Extreme weather has become impossible to ignore—and organizers are being forced to adapt.
For the first time in the history of the World Cup, FIFA began mandating three-minute “hydration breaks” as games across North America carried on amid high temperatures and humidity. The tournament's final was threatened by hazardous wildfire smoke drifting over New York from hundreds of fires burning in Ontario, Canada, as well as northern Minnesota.
The NFL is increasingly favoring roofed and domed stadiums, with nearly two-thirds of league venues expected to see updates by 2030—to the tune of billions of dollars in construction. And in June, a “heat hazard” went into effect for Formula 1’s Austrian Grand Prix, meaning that drivers would be required to have a “driver cooling system” in place in order to compete.
While the organizations behind some of sports’ most popular events are looking to counteract the effects of climate change, athletes are also forced to adapt their training to better acclimate to heat. In the Tour de France, some teams prepared ice baths for riders to utilize immediately after completing a portion of the race. Laura Schifter explained in a recent opinion piece for TIME that even children’s sports will likely be impacted, reshaping the lifelong habits and mindsets young athletes develop.
And the changes ultimately affect those who attend the sporting events. There’s the added strain of attending outdoor sporting events in extreme weather—which often involves long lines leading into the events and long hours in the sun in the stands. There may also be financial consequences, as investments in new facilities or weather adaptations can increase operating costs, which in some cases wind up passed down to fans. Or they might not get to attend at all: Earlier this month, spectators were asked not to watch the last 40 km (25 miles) of the third stage of the Tour de France to reduce the demand on security personnel and free up more resources for the wildfires.
Adaptation measures are only going to become more common in our warming world, experts tell TIME.
“This is the coolest summer that's going to be in our lifetimes,” says Samuel Hampton, senior researcher at the University of Oxford’s Environmental Change Institute. “It's only going to get hotter and hotter for the rest of our lives, and I think the [Tour de France] is already straining in terms of how it can deal with this heat.”
“It's only going to become more challenging,” he added.

title: Champagne and Bullets belongs on the Mount Rushmore of bad movies
summary: There's something about a movie like The Room, Troll 2, or Fateful Findings that I find irresistible. Champagne and Bullets (also released as GetEven and […]
full_text:
There’s something about a movie like The Room, Troll 2, or Fateful Findings that I find irresistible. These sorts of “so bad they’re good” films are marvelous curiosities where ambition far outstrips resources, ability, and self-awareness to become something much greater than the sum of their parts. Champagne and Bullets (also released as GetEven and Road to Revenge) is a film on par with those classics of outsider cinema.
Champagne and Bullets belongs on the Mount Rushmore of bad movies
It’s Steven Seagal meets Neil Breen.
It’s Steven Seagal meets Neil Breen.
The movie is almost entirely the work of one man, John De Hart. Hart wrote, directed, and stars as Rick Bode in the film. He even performs a musical number early in the proceedings — The bizarre “Shimmy Slide.” During the performance, Hart, who was reportedly pumped full of painkillers after throwing out his back, is stiff and looks around the room as if he’s only performing under threat of violence. And somehow, this lifeless performance of a cringy country rocker isn’t the most awkward scene in the movie.
The relationships and interactions between characters in Champagne and Bullets are just as inexplicable and unnatural as those in The Room. Bode and his partner Huck Finney are cops who lose their badges five minutes into the movie. This precipitates the alarmingly quick mental decline of Finney, who is also going through a divorce after discovering his wife has been sleeping around. He fires a handgun through his bills, drinks bleach to get out of prison, and seemingly starts a cult.
Oh, and speaking of cults, a good portion of the plot revolves around the reemergence of Bode’s old girlfriend Cindy, who is fleeing a satanic coven that “sacrificed a human baby.”
While ostensibly an action film, the fight scenes are few and far between, and staged with all the believability of a theme park stunt show. Hart seemed far more interested in cramming in as much gratuitous nudity as possible. There are three uncomfortably long sex scenes with costar Pamela Bryant, who plays Cindy, all set to songs sung by Hart. In total, they take up 12 minutes of runtime in a movie that is only 90 minutes long. One scene that takes place in a jacuzzi apparently even led Hart’s girlfriend at the time to break up with him. (Warning: One scene not involving Hart and Bryant does depict a sexual assault.)
If you’re a fan of bad movies, cult classics, or the podcast How Did This Get Made, you owe it to yourself to go watch Champagne and Bullets. It’s available on Hoopla, Amazon Prime, and Tubi.

title: South Korea trading giant puts receivables onchain in tokenization test with LG CNS
full_text:
South Korea trading giant puts receivables onchain in tokenization test with LG CNS
POSCO International and LG CNS is tapping Injective network to tokenize live commercial invoices, another sign blockchain rails are moving deeper into corporate finance.
- POSCO International is putting live trade receivables on the Injective blockchain in a pilot with LG CNS, aiming to speed up payments between its global subsidiaries.
- By placing receivables on a shared blockchain ledger, the companies aim to create a single, transferable record that embeds compliance rules and reduces reconciliation times for buyers, sellers and banks.
- The initiative, which POSCO plans to move into live production after the pilot, underscores South Korea’s growing corporate adoption of blockchain in areas such as trade finance, stablecoin-based treasury transfers and asset tokenization.
POSCO International, South Korea's largest trading company, has begun tokenizing trade receivables on blockchain in a test that could speed up commercial payments between its global subsidiaries.
The company, which generated $22.2 billion in revenue last year from businesses spanning steel, energy and battery materials, is working with LG CNS, the technology arm of LG Group, to issue, transfer and settle receivables on layer-1 blockchain Injective 
The pilot is using receivables generated by real trade between POSCO's overseas operations and their counterparties rather than simulated transactions.
Trade receivables represent money owed to a company after goods have been shipped but before payment is received. Today, those claims are typically tracked separately by buyers, sellers and banks, with reconciliation often taking days before cash can be released.
The companies said putting receivables on a shared blockchain ledger creates a single record that can be transferred and settled while carrying compliance rules with the asset itself.
"This PoC is significant in that it validated the applicability of AI and blockchain technology based on real trade data and processes," a POSCO International spokesperson said. The firm said it plans to expand the initiative into live production after completing the pilot later this year.
Tokenization expands beyond funds and stocks
Much of the industry's recent attention has centered on tokenizing funds and equities. Asset managers including BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, Apollo, Fidelity, Janus Henderson and Mubadala Capital have all brought funds onchain, betting blockchain infrastructure can streamline issuance, settlement and collateral management. The market for tokenized assets has grown rapidly in the past years to the current size of $35 billion, while Citi estimates the market could reach $5.5 trillion by 2030.
Trade finance is as another promising use case. Receivables represent real commercial obligations between businesses, allowing companies to move working capital more efficiently on blockchain rails while giving banks and financing partners a shared view of the asset.
South Korea has become one of the more active markets for corporate blockchain adoption. Earlier this month, carmaker Hyundai has begun using stablecoins for internal treasury transfers between its U.S. and Mexico operations, while stablecoin issuer Circle recently partnered with Kakao Group and Toss Bank to explore stablecoin payment infrastructure.
With the test on Injective, POSCO and LG CNS are extending that push into global trade finance. LG CNS has previously worked on the Bank of Korea's central bank digital currency pilot and operates tokenization platforms for KOSCOM and Mirae Asset Securities.

title: WEMIX says attacker moved about $724,000 after contract breach
summary: WEMIX suspended bridges, liquidity-pool trading and several services after an attacker compromised a WEMIX$-linked contract and moved 724,198 USDC.e.
full_text:
WEMIX says attacker moved about $724,000 after contract breach
WEMIX suspended bridges, liquidity-pool trading and several services after an attacker compromised a WEMIX$-linked contract and moved 724,198 USDC.e.
Layer-1 blockchain network WEMIX said an attacker moved about 724,000 in USDC.e tokens after compromising ownership of a contract linked to its WEMIX$ stablecoin and issuing tokens without authorization.
The abnormal transactions occurred on Sunday at 9:17 UTC, according to a preliminary incident update from WEMIX. The attacker issued about 5.23 million WEMIX$, which was converted into 30,736 WEMIX and 724,198.27 USDC.e. The USDC.e was then bridged to Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain before being exchanged for assets including Ether and Tether’s USDT and distributed across multiple addresses.
WEMIX said some of the funds were deposited into centralized exchanges. The company identified the attacker’s wallets and requested asset freezes and assistance from exchanges and stablecoin issuers, adding that some exchanges had already frozen addresses linked to the incident.
The company temporarily suspended all bridges connected to its layer-1 network, WEMIX3.0, including Chainlink CCIP and the PLAY Bridge. It also suspended trading in affected liquidity pools, withdrew foundation-provided liquidity, and paused services including the WEMIX$ Module and PNIX decentralized exchange.
WEMIX said the cause and full impact remain under investigation and warned that the preliminary figures could change.

title: Triple-A hot wallet losses climb to $11.8 million as new deposits keep being swept: report
summary: Triple-A said it is investigating and that customer funds are not affected, though it has not fully addressed the incident publicly.
full_text:
Triple-A hot wallet losses climb to $11.8 million as new deposits keep being swept: report
Quick Take
- Onchain investigator Specter said losses from a drain of hot wallets linked to Singapore payments firm Triple-A have reached about $11.8 million, up from an initial estimate of $9.3 million on Friday.
- Triple-A said it is investigating and that customer funds are not affected, though it has not disclosed how the wallets were accessed.
We'd love your feedback.
Losses from an apparent compromise of crypto payments firm Triple-A's hot wallets have grown to roughly $11.8 million, onchain investigator Specter said in a post on X early Sunday.
Specter first flagged the drain at 5:18 p.m. ET on Friday, putting losses at more than $9.3 million and saying the attacker had swapped the assets and bridged them to Ethereum. PeckShield, citing Specter, raised the figure to more than $9.7 million about four and a half hours later.
Specter said Sunday a further $1.8 million had been taken across the Bitcoin and TRON networks, and that new deposits were still arriving at the affected wallets and being drained 31 hours after the first large outflows appeared.
Bitcoin had not previously been named among the affected networks. Earlier reports from Specter and blockchain security firm PeckShield covered Ethereum, TRON, Polygon, Arbitrum, Solana and The Open Network.
The proceeds were pooled at a single Ethereum address, and the screenshot attached to PeckShield’s alert showed the address holding 5,226.67 ETH worth about $9.73 million. It listed eight incoming transfers between 20:35 UTC Friday and 03:03 UTC Saturday, the largest totaling roughly 4,140 ETH.
Triple-A addressed the reports on X on Saturday. "We're actively investigating the situation and will share a formal update once ready. We confirm that customer funds are not impacted," the company said.
Triple A Technologies Pte. Ltd. is licensed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore as a major payment institution and processes stablecoin payments for merchants that settle in local currency. Its European arm, Paytop SAS, holds payment institution and crypto-asset service provider licenses in France, and the group is registered as a money services business in the U.S. and Canada.
Since Oct. 4, 2024, Singapore’s Payment Services Regulations have required licensed digital payment token service providers to safeguard customer assets in trust accounts, while MAS guidance calls for those assets to be held at blockchain addresses separate from the firms’ own holdings. Triple-A has not identified what the affected wallets contained, saying only that customer funds were not impacted.
Triple-A has not published the promised formal update in its newsroom, where the latest entry remains a July 15 announcement that Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority granted the company in-principle approval for broker-dealer services. That release described compliance as Triple-A's second-largest department after engineering.
The incident follows two other large crypto exploits disclosed this week. AFX Trade, a protocol on Arbitrum, lost about $24.15 million in USDC through its custody bridge in an exploit disclosed Wednesday. The Verus-Ethereum bridge lost roughly $7.54 million the same day, its second breach since May.
The Block was unable to reach Triple-A for comment.

title: First teaser for Apple TV's Neuromancer debuts at SDCC
summary: Plus Mike Flanagan's Carrie teaser, trailers for Dark Matter S2 and Matchbox the Movie, and Marvel news.
full_text:
Apple TV is fast eclipsing HBO as the go-to platform for prestige TV, especially science fiction, with standout fare like Slow Horses, Severance, Foundation, For All Mankind, Murderbot, Silo, Pluribus, and Widow’s Bay, among others. Add the upcoming Neuromancer series to that list, an adaption of William Gibson’s hugely influential 1984 cyberpunk novel of the same name. The streaming platform released a short teaser during San Diego Comic-Con, and visually it looks fantastic, even based on one minute of footage.
Saturday’s various SDCC panels also gave us a teaser for Prime Video’s Carrie; trailers for Dark Matter S2 and Matchbox: The Movie; and a bit of Marvel casting news.
Fans of Gibson’s book already know the Neuromancer story; we’ll have to wait and see how closely the series will adhere to the novel. Per the official logline, the series “follows a damaged, top-rung super-hacker named Case who is thrust into a web of digital espionage with his partner Molly, a razor-girl assassin with mirrored eyes, aiming to pull a heist on a corporate dynasty with untold secrets.” Callum Taylor, best known as Theseus Scamander in the Fantastic Beasts franchise, stars as Case, alongside Briana Middleton (The Inheritance) as Molly.
The cast also includes a blond-haired Mark Strong as Armitage; Joseph Lee as Hideo; Clemence Poesy as Marie-France Tessier; Peter Sarsgaard as John Ashpool; Emma Laird as Linda Lee; Max Irons as Jean Tessier-Ashpool; Dane DeHaan as Peter Riviera; Marc Menchaca as Dixie Flatline; Andre de Shields as Julius Deane; and Isabella Pappas as Mitchell.
Neuromancer premieres on January 22, 2027, on Apple TV+.
Carrie
I’m a staunch fan of Mike Flanagan‘s burgeoning horror portfolio, and he has a particular affinity for the works of Stephen King, as evidenced by his film adaptations of Gerald’s Game and Doctor Sleep. But I confess to being a wee bit skeptical about his new Prime Video miniseries based on Carrie, King’s most famous character, immortalized by Sissy Spacek in the 1976 film. We don’t need another disappointing remake so what story is there left to tell—especially stretched out over six episodes?

title: 淺談 Xbox 大裁員：Game Pass 內容也大裁員？
summary: 原本外界以為 Xbox 會因作風明快的 Asha Sharma 上任後有番新氣象，沒想到近來再度傳出大裁員，且 […]
full_text:
原本外界以為 Xbox 會因作風明快的 Asha Sharma 上任後有番新氣象，沒想到近來再度傳出大裁員，且是部門成立後最大規模裁員和重整，包含許多當初重金收購的明星工作室也難逃一劫，讓人不禁擔心 Xbox 力推的 Game Pass 是否也會因重整喪失競爭力？
當初Xbox前掌門人Phil Spencer大肆併購遊戲工作室，最核心目的就是壯大XBOX Game Pass（XGP）的生態系與內容庫，並藉由訂閱制護城河，主機大戰能對抗Sony PlayStation的領先地位。畢竟Xbox One時代，微軟最大問題就是缺乏強勢的第一方獨佔遊戲（First-Party Exclusives）。看著對手Sony靠《戰神》或《秘境探險》系列等獨佔大作屢創佳績，Phil Spencer意識到要吸引玩家加入XGP，不能只靠第三方老遊戲或獨立遊戲，必須要有殺手級大作。
故Phil Spence開啟一連串令人咋舌的遊戲商併購之旅，包含收購手握《Forza》系列的Playground Games、擁有《Fallout》系列的Bethesda，以及堪稱MMORPG大作產生器的動視暴雪（Activision Blizzard）皆收入微軟麾下。
Phil Spencer認為要讓訂閱制成功，關鍵在持續且穩定提供高品質的新內容。如果只仰賴跟第三方發行商買版權放上XGP，長期授權成本極高且不穩定。將開發商買下來成為「自家人」，微軟就能完全掌控遊戲發行節奏，確保每月、每季都有重量級新遊戲加入XGP，建立強大的使用者黏著度。
然而理想和現實總是有落差。現代3A大作開發時間動輒數年，開發成本呈指數上升。微軟買下許多工作室（如Double Fine、Compulsion Games等）遲遲未能交出能動訂閱數大幅增長的神作，反而成了沉重的財務負擔。
雪上加霜的是Game Pass經歷前幾年爆發性成長後，近期已達瓶頸。當願意訂閱的核心玩家都已加入，再怎麼花大錢買工作室，也很難再大幅拉升訂閱數。甚至近來爆出微軟高層開始反彈「首日上XGP」策略。因開發成本高昂的3A大作如果只靠訂閱費回收，往往難以回本，更直接吃掉遊戲本該有的龐大買斷制銷售利潤。
加上近來記憶體暴漲導致硬體成本大幅上升使銷量陡降，微軟再也無法容忍Xbox部門只燒錢不賺錢的狀態，才導致新執行長Asha Sharma必須快刀斬亂麻，大裁員與剝離工作室。
所以Game Pass內容是否可能因這次大規模重整而導致競爭力降低？以Asha Sharma獲利至上的原則和專注旗艦3A遊戲開發的大方向，Game Pass的確很有可能減少很多Day One遊戲，畢竟Xbox現在再度邁入轉型期，之後Xbox能否削減成本與維持遊戲品質之間取得平衡，將成為決定生態系能否長存的關鍵。
（首圖來源：Xbox）

title: UK's most parched regions miss chance for rain ahead of next heatwave
summary: Much of the UK continues to experience very dry conditions after a summer marked by low rainfall and recurring heatwaves.
full_text:
UK's most parched regions miss chance for rain ahead of next heatwave
- Published
Some of the driest regions of the UK have missed their chances for rain ahead of another heatwave beginning this week.
Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall over the weekend, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.
But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.
It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.
The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 35C (95F) in south-east England.
In advance of the high temperatures, heat health alerts have been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).
The south-west, south-east, London, East of England, West and East Midlands and Yorkshire and The Humber are all under the alerts from 9:00 BST on Tuesday 28 July until 9:00 BST on Friday 31 July.
The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.
- Is there a hosepipe ban in my area? What you need to know - Published3 days ago
 
- What is the definition of a heatwave? - Published24 April 2025
 
How hot will it get this week?
The hot weather will initially be focused on central and eastern England by Tuesday before spreading slightly northwards and westwards into midweek.
Temperatures in England and Wales are forecast to rise to around 25-32C for much of next week.
However, Wednesday is likely to be the hottest day, with readings of 30-35C across the Midlands, southern and eastern England.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will generally remain cooler and showery with temperatures in the high teens or low to mid-twenties Celsius.
Current forecasts suggest that the intense heat across southern and central Britain this week will be short-lived compared to previous heatwaves this summer.
No substantial rain on the horizon for driest regions
Over the weekend, rainfall was focused mainly across the north and west of the UK.
Meanwhile, the driest locations - including central, southern and eastern England - saw little, if any, meaningful rainfall.
As the spell of hot weather develops across England and Wales, the lack of significant rain means dry ground and low soil moisture levels are likely to become an increasing concern.
The driest parts of England and Wales have seen exceptionally low rainfall so far this month.
Some areas, particularly in parts of north Wales and southern and eastern England, have recorded only a few millimetres of rain or even less.
Wisley in Surrey has been one of the driest locations in southeast England with 39 days of no rainfall as of 26 July.
In the driest spots, totals have been below 2% of the average July rainfall.

title: Girlguiding unveils first major uniform redesign since 1990
summary: Under the new rules, members will be able to wear a top from the new range with their own trousers.
full_text:
Girlguiding unveils first major uniform redesign since 1990
- Published
Girlguiding has unveiled the first major redesign of its uniform in more than 30 years, with the aim of allowing its members the "freedom to express themselves".
Under the new, pared-back approach, members will only be required to wear a top from the new range to be considered "in uniform".
The new range has been inspired by feedback from thousands of Guides, Rainbows, Brownies and Rangers which suggested they valued choice and the ability to express their own style.
Girlguiding chief executive Felicity Oswald said "practicality, comfort and sustainability" were at the centre of the redesign, which updates the 1990 version of the uniform.
The organisation said the uniform combines the charity's heritage with modern colours and prints.
The range is made up of 30 items of clothing, 15 accessories and neckerchiefs - with prices starting at £12, for a T-shirt.
Design features include hidden pockets in waist bands, thumb holes, and badge sashes which double as cross-body bags.
This is the first time in 30 years Girlguiding has updated its entire range at the same time.
Oswald said the range was "all about providing girls with the freedom to express themselves, whilst feeling part of our amazing organisation".
Members do not have to buy the new range straightaway, the website explains, and they can continue to wear the old uniform until they need a replacement.
A Girlguiding survey in June of 2,000 girls aged six to 16 in the UK found that 93% said they felt most comfortable when able to choose how they styled themselves.
Angellica Bell, a Girlguiding ambassador and presenter, said the new design gives "girls and volunteers the freedom to style it the way that suits them".
She added: "The new uniform empowers girls and volunteers to embrace their individuality."

title: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
summary: The vast majority of people - particularly women - answer a survey saying they'd take the certainty over chance.
full_text:
Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
- Published
You have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1m.
Which would you choose?
The vast majority decide on taking the £50k, according to a survey of thousands of people by YouGov. Women voted 82% in favour of the guaranteed cash.
The poll has sparked a debate about why Brits appear more risk-averse than people in the US.
So why are the results so clear-cut, and what are the financial and psychological factors at play?
Sadly, there is little chance of ever having such a choice, but there are some interesting lessons for how we manage our money nonetheless.
Do you agree with the majority?
Nearly three-quarters (73%) of the 4,600 adults asked in the survey said they would take the £50,000 now.
Just over a fifth (21%) went for the chance of £1m and, 6% of those asked sat on the fence and simply couldn't decide.
The gender split in the results is striking. Some 82% of women opted for the £50,000, compared with 63% of men.
This chimes with other research which suggests that men are twice as likely to invest in stocks and shares than women, external, and women are more likely to subscribe to cash ISAs than men, external.
Does the choice depend on how much you earn?
Lots of people might opt for the £50,000 guarantee, deciding that it is a life-changing amount of money in itself.
After all, it is £10,000 more than the median average earnings for full-time workers in the UK for an entire year, according to official statistics, external.
But younger people generally earn less and yet, according to this survey, external, those aged 18 to 24 are more willing to take the bet on £1m than any other age group.
Some 28% go for the coin flip, compared with just 11% among the over-65s - their grandparents' generation.
There is a different tipping point for everyone. Repeat the survey but instead guarantee £5 or offer a 50/50 chance for a £100, and most people will probably go for the £100 bet. After all, lots of people bet at least £2 a week hoping for a National Lottery win.
As those amounts rise, so your appetite for risk becomes clear.
Why not just invest the £50k?
One choice is to take the guaranteed £50,000 and hope it grows over time.
Saving the money would be helped by the magic of compound interest.
Alternatively, you could take more of a risk, but potentially with greater reward, by investing the money.
What has happened in the past will not necessarily happen in the future when it comes to investments.
But you'd have had to have invested your £50,000 in a typical global fund just under 38 years ago for it to be worth £1m today, according to Sarah Coles, of investment firm AJ Bell.
Is it all in the mind?
We are hardwired, says Coles, to go for the guaranteed £50,000.
That's because we feel losses more acutely than gains, she says.
"The thrill of potentially winning £1m is felt less strongly than the fear of giving up a guaranteed £50,000 and ending up with nothing," she says.
In other words, having £50k and knowing you might have won £1m will play on your mind.
But it is not as bad as having a crack at £1m and knowing you've given up enough for an average deposit to buy a home in the West Midlands, external.

title: UK papers: Youth benefits 'crack down' and Gatwick 'Fly and dry'
summary: Andy Burnham's latest policy plans dominate many of Monday's newspapers.
full_text: Youth benefits 'crack down' and Gatwick 'Fly and dry'Published1 hour agoImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's latest policy plans lead several front pages. "PM to crack down on youth benefits" is the Daily Telegraph's headline, reporting that "payments may be stopped unless training or voluntary work is done" as part of the new administration's efforts to "reduce the country's £333bn welfare bill" and "find billions of pounds for spending on social care and defence". "We will always support those who genuinely need it", said a spokesman for the Department of Work and Pensions.Image caption, "Young people who take up part-time work on minimum wage earn £100 less than those claiming sickness benefits", is the Times' top story. Using its own analysis, the paper says more than 87,000 16 and 17-year-olds are claiming personal independence benefit (Pip). The government told the paper: "Pip, as designed in 2013, is no longer fit for purpose".Image caption, The i Paper tops with its own reporting that the new government is "actively considering options to replace council tax and stamp duty", writing that more than 100 Labour MPs support "two alternatives – a proportional property tax and a land value tax". Burnham "rules out general early election", the paper adds, quoting the new leader: "I don't think people want it". Image caption, The Guardian headlines on the new foreign secretary Ed Miliband vowing "to give UK 'global leadership' role on climate crisis" by "taking up the country's seat on the board at the World Bank". The position is usually delegated to a junior minister, the paper explains.Image caption, Another reshuffled cabinet minister, Wes Streeting, unveils his promise to "quit if defence plan falls short" as he takes on the post of defence secretary, the Daily Mail writes. Streeting, who held the health portfolio before stepping down in May, made the conditional promise as Burnham "refuses to commit to 3% funding increase by 2030", according to the paper.Image caption, The Financial Times leads with defence companies' "push" towards tech start-ups in order to "adapt to the rapidly evolving face of modern warfare", citing new venture capital rounds launched by Lockheed Martin and BAE Systems. The companies have "long-standing ties to western governments and militaries", the paper explains.Image caption, "No go at Gatwick for thousands after water outage with loos blocked up and taps all off," reads the Metro's lead story, under the headline "Fly and dry". Expanding on the "grim start" to travelling families, it writes, "drinking fountains were out of action", "there were queues for toilets, which could not be flushed" and "crowds were forced to sit on the floor". Image caption, "Police 'waste' millions on diversity schemes", says the Daily Express. It reports on new findings from a conservative think tank, which says £631m was spent on diversity, equality and inclusion activities since 2020 across police forces. Such funds "could instead have been used to fight crime" or recruited "thousands of new officers", according to the paper, quoting the report's author David Spencer. Chair of the National Police Chiefs' Council's DEI committee, chief constable Rachel Kearton, told the paper that "understanding the communities we serve" is essential.Image caption, A "grieving mum's plea" leads the Daily Mirror, whose daughter died after contracting E.Coli – a potentially harmful bacteria found in infected food or unclean water. She is urging the new prime minister "to crack down on firms pumping sewage into sea & rivers". Image caption, "Huge rise in drivers filling up without paying" is the Daily Star's lead, writing that "nearly 800 people a day are nicking petrol from forecourts". It quips: "Tanks for nothing".Image caption, Finally, the Sun leads with something that will excite soccer "ace" Cristiano Ronaldo's fans – he is due to play himself in a TV drama. "Lights! Camera! Act Ron!" is the playful headline. title: Losing my leg has elevated my life, says world champion surfer
summary: Llywelyn Williams says anything is possible with any kind of disability.
full_text:
Losing my leg has elevated my life, says world champion surfer
- Published
Four-time world champion adaptive surfer Llywelyn Williams says losing his leg as a teenager elevated his life.
Surfing played a pivotal role in his recovery and in the years since losing a leg after being hit by a car in 2011.
It had been a passion of the then 16-year-old prior to the accident - and it was not going to stop him despite being severely injured while out skateboarding.
In fact, he recalled coming around from a coma in hospital amid a dream that a surfboard came between him and a bright light "like you see in the movies".
"It wasn't my time," said Williams, from Abersoch, Gwynedd.
A friend asked him what he wanted to do while he lay in his hospital bed; he wanted to get back in the water - and go surfing in Australia.
"The rehab was to drive myself to get back into the ocean," said Williams, known as Sponge by friends.
"As soon as I got back in the ocean, I felt like I was born again.
"When the board and you connect perfect on the wave, it just feels like you're flying."
His mother, Eirian Parry, described the "beautiful moment" his friends carried him into the sea as he continued his recovery following the amputation.
But she still recalled with visible emotion the time she and Williams' father faced up to a "nightmare" - when doctors asked them to sign a consent form to amputate their son's right leg.
David Williams told BBC documentary Our Lives: Beyond the Waves it was the hardest decision of his life "but it was the only way to save" his son's life.
"To think he was nearly dead on the side of the road when the accident happened... to being the world champion," he said.
"Once he got his first wave back, there was no stopping him."
His father can also remember tough times early into his son's recovery, one in which he told him he had to be strong while at a low point, and then took himself off and cried in the room next to his son.
"The way my parents have brought me up is you've just got to get on with it so, yeah, I had one leg and that was it," said Williams.
He works as a digger driver in the family construction business when not surfing.
"I've learned how to do everything with one leg, except to be able to use a wheelbarrow," said Williams with a wry smile.
"When I turned 18 I wheelchaired my way into the kitchen and said we're heading off to Australia.
"We did a year out there travelling around the coast surfing, living in a camper van.
"To be able to go back there now every year for a competition is just brilliant."
In March, he won the 2026 Bright Sky Australian Pro Adaptive Surfing Championship as the kneeling champion and proudly held the Welsh flag aloft on the beach at Byron Bay, New South Wales.
And he was third in the North Shore Prosthetics Hawaiian Surfing Championships in May.
He self funds participation in surfing competitions and has been thankful for his supporters close to home.
Williams has also been lobbying with others for his sport to be included in a future Paralympics Games.
"Surfing has been a huge part of my recovery and the adaptive surfing community has helped me so much," he said.
"Disability for me has elevated my life - anything is possible if you have any kind of disability."
Our Lives: Beyond the Waves
After losing his leg as a teenager, surfer Llywelyn Williams became a four-times para surfing world champion. Now he’s on top of the adaptive surfing world, the challenge is to stay there.

title: 'South Asian programmes helped us settle into our new lives'
summary: Early South Asian programming included music and practical tips to settle into British life.
full_text:
'South Asian programmes helped us settle into our new lives'
- Published
For the first generation of South Asian migrants to the UK, dedicated radio and television broadcasts by the BBC were a lifeline.
As well as lighter content such as music, the early output included practical advice to help new arrivals settle into their lives in areas such as West Yorkshire, where many South Asian families were attracted by jobs in the textile industry.
Sixty years on, three generations have shared their memories of South Asian programming and spoken about how it shaped them.
When Nirmala Rani arrived in the Leeds suburb of Hyde Park in 1979, life felt quiet and unfamiliar. She was a Punjabi speaker from India and knew few people in England.
Aged 17, Nirmala had come to Leeds to join her husband, whose family had already settled there. Like many South Asian families then, she followed relatives who had moved first to build a new life.
"When a letter came from home, we'd read it 10 times."
With no telephone and no relatives nearby, each letter was a lifeline.
She was adjusting to a new country, new culture, and a loneliness that came from being far from the sounds and language she understood.
The BBC had already begun making programmes for South Asian audiences. One of the first, 'Apna Hi Ghar Samajhiye' (Make Yourself at Home), offered language lessons, music and advice.
By the late 1960s, a magazine programme for South Asian viewers, 'Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan', had become a weekend fixture.
"We'd wait the whole week to hear one Hindi song," Nirmala says. "Music was food for our souls."
Sunday mornings became something to look forward to. Families gathered around the television with homemade food.
"We'd make chole puri or aloo tikki. It felt nice, everybody sat enjoying together.
"It got rid of the loneliness."
Those same programmes meant just as much to Krishna Devi, who arrived in 1967 and lived in Harehills, another inner-city neighbourhood in Leeds.
Krishna was also just 17 when she came from India, joining her husband and his family.
"It wasn't easy," Krishna says. "We didn't understand English and they didn't understand Punjabi."
One programme helped new arrivals learn the basics: 'Look, Listen and Speak', a BBC English learning series widely used at that time.
"They used to teach us word by word. They taught us how to cross the road. Look left, right."
Even simple tasks could feel unfamiliar.
"When I went to the shops, I didn't know how much things cost. I'd put the money out on my hand and let the shopkeeper take however much it was."
Like Nirmala, the programme she looked forward to most was Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan.
"There was one Hindi song in that half hour. We waited for it."
Asked why those songs mattered so much, her answer is simple.
"Because it was our language. That half hour made us forget everything else."
Her Sundays followed a familiar pattern: chai, parathas and three generations gathered around a television.
Experiences like Krishna's were shared in living rooms across the country, but inside the BBC, broadcaster and Asian Network pioneer Anita Bhalla was pushing for something more than comfort.
She wanted representation, and a voice.
"When I started, we didn't exist," she says. "There was nobody like me, except in the specialist programmes."
Those early shows mattered because they were the only place migrant families could see or hear anything familiar.
"There was nothing else where people could connect with home, with language, culture, anything."
She later helped shape the early Asian Network in the late 1980s.
"We were no longer new arrivals. We were integrated communities. So, what was our voice? That's what we were trying to find."
She pushed for South Asians not just on screen, but behind it.
"Where were the people behind the scenes? That's where the real power was."
Reflecting on young South Asians entering the industry today, she says: "I hope their ambitions aren't capped. They should be everywhere."
For Yasmin Shabir, who grew up in the Leeds suburb of Armley in the 1990s, programmes like 'Network East' and 'Goodness Gracious Me' helped a new generation of British Asians see themselves on screen.
Raised in a Pakistani household, she remembers these programmes as a weekly link to the culture her parents had grown up with.
"Those programmes were our only way of actually finding out what was going on in Bollywood and the entertainment world.
"Seeing Salman Khan on the BBC was surreal. We were like, 'Wow, how did they get him?' "
But it was 'Goodness Gracious Me' that resonated most.
"The competitive aunties comparing their children, 'my son's doing this...well, my son's doing that'
"We could relate to the characters. It felt like real life.
"They'd say a word in Hindi and I'd think, 'I know that word.'
"It felt like it was made for us. They brought a bit of flavour to life."
By the early 2000s, British Asian culture was breaking into the mainstream.
In the middle of that shift was Bobby Friction, who now presents on BBC Asian Network.
"The revolutions of the 1990s paved the way for the riches of the early noughties," he remembers.
" 'Goodness Gracious Me', for us, was monumental - that specific British Desi humour was on national TV."
Seeing members of the cast who were from the same parts of London as he was felt, he says, "like the revolution wasn't just in my head, it was happening across the country".
"In 2002, Radio 1 decided to do a South Asian music show, and Nihal Arthanayake and I were chosen to present it.
"My ambition since the age of 15 was to be on Radio 1 playing South Asian music."
That same year, Asian Network went national, and Desi DNA launched soon after.
"Suddenly you're in this new era which has already started when the other era hasn't even finished yet.
"At that time, if you were young and South Asian just coming of age, it was very, very different compared to even 10 years before."
For millennials like Tasmiyah Manan from Oakwood in north Leeds, South Asian broadcasting didn't just entertain; it shaped how she understood herself.
She remembers watching Network East Late, Desi DNA and tuning into Asian Network as teenager, long before streaming and TikTok reshaped how music travelled.
"It was the main station playing the music I grew up listening to. I connected to it, the songs, the language, the artists."
Seeing presenter Noreen Khan on air inspired her.
"She's been a staple in my life. Seeing her in the media inspired me to want to go into the media."
She loved the fusion artists like Jay Sean blending R&B, Punjabi, Hindi and English into something that felt exactly like her life.
"I was born in England, I'm British Pakistani, I live my life with fusion. Those artists sounded like us."
Comedy mattered too. Shows like 'The Kumars at No. 42' reflected her world.
"The paratha smoke filling the kitchen, the brutally honest elders, that was us.
"When I see someone like Anita Rani in the media, it makes me feel seen.
"It means we've finally made it to the mainstream."
"If they can do it, I can. It's representation. It's connection. It's my identity."
When Arzu Dutta was growing up in Castleford in the 2000s, representation still felt limited.
Now a BBC Look North reporter and presenter on Radio Leeds, she can see how far things have changed.
She watched Indian entertainment channels at home, but it was the BBC that quietly shaped her British identity, especially the moments she shared with her dad before school.
"My dad would make chai, and we'd sit and watch the news, and watch Naga Munchetty presenting.
"It forms your subconscious of who you are and how you view yourself and the heights you can reach."
Today, she says British Asian identity feels more defined.
"We are at a place where the hyphen between British and Asian is really important.
"As long as South Asian people exist, South Asian broadcasting will matter because you can relate to it.
"I don't walk around thinking, 'I'm Indian.' I just am."

title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
summary: Some students said they are having to hide their Jewish identity, fearing physical and verbal abuse.
full_text:
'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
- Published
Some Jewish students have said they feel antisemitism has become "normalised" at UK universities and they routinely hide signs of their identity for fear of abuse.
Students at more than 10 universities in England and Wales told the BBC they had faced hostility, and warned of a "culture of antisemitism" on campuses.
A report into the issue by the Union of Jewish students in March 2026 called for new enforceable standards for how universities investigate and punish hate crime.
Universities UK, which represents more than 140 higher education institutions, said universities were working to improve support, reporting and campus safety for Jewish students.
Cardiff University student Oliver, 21, said being Jewish had always been a central part of his identity.
He described his first week at the university in 2023 as "terrifying", because it had coincided with the 7 October attacks when Hamas militants attacked Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking hundreds hostage.
Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, in which it is estimated more than 70,000 Palestinians have died.
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.
Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.
"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.
"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"
Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.
Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".
"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.
"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.
"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."
Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.
Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.
Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".
It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.
It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.
'Hiding their identity'
Oliver is not alone in feeling this way.
There are about 9,000 Jewish students in the UK and reported antisemitic incidents on UK campuses rose by more than 400%, from 53 in the 2022-23 academic year, to 272 in 2023-24, according to the Community Security Trust, which monitors antisemitism in the UK.
Universities UK acknowledged antisemitism is a growing challenge.
Its chief executive, Vivienne Stern, said her organisation was committed to tackling campus antisemitism and was actively working with Jewish students to bring about change.
"I think that Jewish students should be able to wear signs that they are Jewish," she said.
"They should be able to wear their Star of David necklace or their kippah, and they should be able to celebrate Jewish life."
Daniel, the incoming Jewish Society vice-president at Manchester University, said Jewish students in the city had started "hiding their identity" after the 7 October attacks and later the Heaton Park attack in October 2025, when two Jewish people were killed after a car was driven into pedestrians outside a synagogue.
He said antisemitic slogans and swastikas had been daubed on walls and a swastika drawn on a fridge at a house party after partygoers had discovered the host was Jewish.
Daniel said he was aware a Jewish student wearing a kippah had also been warned by staff not to enter an academic building during protests for fear of their safety.
"To be Jewish at university is to have an identity that is inherently politicised by everyone around you," he said.
"That becomes very exhausting because it's a very difficult place to navigate."
A University of Manchester spokesperson said previous incidents of offensive graffiti on campus were removed promptly, with involvement from police.
They said the unversity took antisemitism "extremely seriously" and investigated it, and that the university has worked closely with civic and faith leaders to promote dialogue and understanding between communities.
They added: "We are working with Jewish students, staff and community representatives to strengthen our response to antisemitism.
"There is however more to do, and we are working with the Antisemitism Policy Trust and other universities to share learning, identify effective practice and strengthen our collective response to antisemitism."
The president of Swansea University's Jewish Society said she had to alert local counter-terrorism officers when organising routine activities for the society.
"I don't think anyone running, say, the Manga [Japanese comic books] Society has to consider whether there's a hate crime risk from having a stall," said Aviva.
"I'm a 20-year-old just going about university life. Getting calls from the police to tell me there isn't a terrorism risk isn't a normal experience."
Swansea University said it supports students through dedicated wellbeing, academic and faith services, and is maintaining a zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination.
A recent survey, external of 1,000 students commissioned by the Union of Jewish Students, conducted by JL Partners between January and February 2026, said Jewish students were being "isolated by their peers" because of the Israel-Palestine conflict.
The poll suggested "apathy" towards antisemitism, with one in four (25%) students saying they did not care "very much" or "at all" if students are able to be open about their Jewish identity.
Lloyd said he felt vulnerable for the first time after he had moved to Bangor University last year and witnessed students chanting "you're a Jew, Jew, Jew" at another student.
Lloyd said it was handled "really well" when he raised it with the society responsible.
But he said incidents like this could leave Jewish students feeling unsure about how and when to challenge antisemitic behaviour.
"I'm lucky. I'm a big guy, and I don't feel particularly scared for my physical safety," he said.
"[But] it's enough to make me very hesitant, most of the time, to say that I'm Jewish."
Bangor University said it had a zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination, and any formal complaints would be thoroughly investigated.
Oliver has now graduated from university and said that, in his final year, he started wearing his Star of David again.
"I deserve to be here, I've earned my place, and I'm going to get the degree I've earned."
